nameStory: The Powder-headed Tube Lichen gets its name from its unique hollow, tube-like lobes that often split open to reveal a powdery white interior. When the tips of these tubes crack or break, they look like they've been dusted with flour or baby powder, giving this lichen its distinctive "powder-headed" appearance.
description: Powder-headed Tube Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms grayish patches on tree bark and rocks. Its most striking feature is its collection of hollow, inflated lobes that look like tiny gray-green tubes clustered together. These tube-like structures can grow several inches across in mature specimens, creating distinctive cushion-like colonies that stand out from flatter lichens.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive hollow, inflated lobes that feel like tiny balloons when gently pressed - they're actually tubular and often split at the tips

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to pale gray on top, with a jet-black underside that's visible where lobes curl up or break

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth and somewhat shiny when dry, with a leathery feel - the surface may have small white powdery spots (soredia) especially at lobe tips

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual tube-like lobes are typically 1-3 inches long, forming patches that can spread several inches across on suitable surfaces

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Most commonly found on the bark of deciduous trees, occasionally on rocks, usually attached at the base while the tubes extend outward

habitat: Look for Powder-headed Tube Lichen on the bark of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on oak, maple, and birch. It prefers somewhat open woodlands and forest edges where there's good air circulation, and can occasionally be found on large boulders or rock outcrops. This species tends to grow in areas with moderate humidity rather than the dampest forest floors.

seasonality.spring: Easiest to spot when spring rains make the gray-green color more vibrant and prominent against still-bare tree bark. The hollow tubes may be more obvious as they absorb moisture.
seasonality.summer: Can appear duller and more gray during dry periods, but the distinctive tubular structure remains the key identifying feature. Look for the characteristic split tube tips with white powdery interiors.
seasonality.fall: Often stands out beautifully against colorful autumn leaves, and the cooler, moister conditions may enhance the greenish tint of the upper surface.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round and may actually be easier to spot on snow-covered branches. The black underside creates striking contrast against white snow when lobes curl upward.

funFact: This lichen's tube-like lobes are actually tiny air chambers that help it survive dry periods - when moisture is scarce, these inflated structures can collapse slightly to reduce water loss, then puff back up like miniature balloons when conditions improve!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its relative the Hooded Tube Lichen, but Powder-headed Tube Lichen has more distinctly inflated, balloon-like lobes that often split to show white powder inside, while Hooded Tube Lichen has flatter, more hood-shaped lobes. Memory trick: "Powder-headed puffs up, Hooded stays flat."
contextualKnowledge: This species was first scientifically described in 1840, making it one of the earlier-recognized tube lichens. The genus name Hypogymnia literally means "naked underneath," referring to the bare black underside that distinguishes these lichens from many other leafy species.
compareHints: Among the tube lichens in New England, Powder-headed Tube Lichen has the most inflated, balloon-like lobes compared to its relatives. Hooded Tube Lichen has flatter, more wrinkled lobes, while Freckled Tube Lichen is smaller with distinctive dark spots. Lattice Tube Lichen has a more net-like pattern of interconnected lobes rather than the distinct separate tubes of the Powder-headed species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tube lichen relatives, Hooded Tube Lichen has those distinctive pepper-like black dots scattered across its surface and more pronounced upward-curling edges.

Freckled Tube Lichen differs from Hooded Tube Lichen by having scattered dark spots rather than smooth surfaces, and from Powder-headed Tube Lichen by lacking the powdery white soredia (reproductive dust) at the lobe tips.
Unlike its relative the Hooded Tube Lichen which has more inflated, hood-like lobes, Lattice Tube Lichen has distinctly hollow, narrower tubes.
